Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Vignette:
Andreas sat rigidly in his chair, his eyes scanning the room with a mixture of wariness and desperation. It had been three years since Hurricane Maria ravaged Puerto Rico, where he was serving as a military medic. The memories still felt like an open wound, refusing to heal. He recalled the sound of rain lashing against the makeshift medical tent, threatening to collapse it at any moment. The cries for help, the screams of pain, and the eerie silence that followed were etched in his mind like a scar. As he worked tirelessly to triage patients, Andreas's medic training kicked in, but nothing could have prepared him for the sheer scale of devastation. He remembered the feeling of being completely overwhelmed, unsure of where to start or how to make a difference. The faces of those he couldn't save haunted him still – their eyes frozen in terror, their bodies broken and battered. Andreas's hypervigilance had become a constant companion since then. Loud noises made him jump; unexpected sounds sent his heart racing. He was always on edge, waiting for the other shoe to drop. Even in the safety of his own home, he couldn't shake off the feeling that disaster was lurking just around the corner. His inability to relax had taken a toll on his relationships – or what was left of them. His wife, Maria, had passed away six months after the hurricane, and Andreas felt lost without her. When memories of the event resurfaced, Andreas felt like he was reliving that terror all over again. He tried to push them away, but they lingered, refusing to be extinguished. The sequence of events was jumbled in his mind – a confused mess of images and sounds. He remembered the smell of mud and decay, the feeling of being knee-deep in water, but the rest was a blur. The trauma had also left Andreas questioning everything he thought he knew about the world. His faith in humanity's inherent goodness had been shaken; his trust in institutions had crumbled. Nothing felt meaningful anymore – not his work as a medic, not his relationships, not even his own identity. He felt like a stranger to himself, unsure of what he believed or who he was supposed to be. As the months went by, Andreas's avoidance behaviors became more entrenched. He stopped attending social gatherings, fearing that someone would trigger a memory or make him feel vulnerable. His performance at work suffered; he found it difficult to concentrate on even the simplest tasks. His commanding officer had suggested counseling, but Andreas was hesitant – what if they didn't understand? What if they judged him? It wasn't until his best friend from the military called, expressing concern about Andreas's increasing isolation, that he realized he needed help. The conversation had left him feeling raw and exposed, but also – for the first time in years – a glimmer of hope. Maybe there was a way to make sense of this mess; maybe there was a way to find meaning again. As Andreas sat in the therapist's office, his eyes locked onto the floor, he knew that the journey ahead would be arduous. But for the first time since Maria's passing, he felt willing to confront the darkness head-on – no matter how terrifying it seemed.
